extracted.intended_audience: students, practitioners, and general readers interested in public relations, propaganda, and media history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and evaluative standards for practicing or assessing public-relations/propaganda work (techniques, ethics, media strategy, and messaging) as described in Edward Bernays / Propaganda–style guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat personality as an objective fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The propagandist must treat personality as he would treat any other objective fact within his province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a public figure has decided what ends he wishes to achieve, he must regard himself objectively and present an outward picture of himself which is consistent with his real character and his aims. A personality may create circumstances (e.g., Lindbergh creating goodwill) or events may create a personality (e.g., the Cuban War creating Roosevelt as a political figure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a public personality to typify organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The public instinctively demands a personality to typify a conspicuous corporation or enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations counsel should dramatize and shape personalities so they typify and personify a company or idea; misuse (over-reporting private matters) can make a public personality absurd (example: firing partner for divorce because public perceives private failure as professional failure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use every available medium — be alert to all means of propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who would most effectively transmit his message to the public must be alert to make use of all the means of propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means cited include motion pictures, parades, radio, television and other avenues; a new product may be announced by a distant motion picture parade or a manufacturer may speak into a million homes via radio/TV. Choose media appropriate to reach audiences effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame publicity as news rather than paid advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays refined and popularized the use of the press release and convinced industries that the news, not advertising, was the best medium to carry their message to an unsuspecting public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create newsworthy events and secure unpaid news coverage (e.g., staging the 'Torches of Freedom' parade, covering Dodge radio programs) rather than relying solely on paid ads; present staged events as news to gain credibility and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and dramatize events to secure coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel is an Emersonian-like creator of events that dramatized new concepts and perceptions and even influenced the actions of leaders and groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage spectacles and events (parades, breakfasts, exhibitions, jubilees) that the press will cover as news—examples: Easter parade for Lucky Strike, 'pancake breakfast' for Coolidge, Light's Golden Jubilee—understand that such events may be contrived to appear spontaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage third-party authorities and opinion leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect use of 'third party authorities' to plead his clients' causes: 'If you can influence the leaders... you automatically influence the group which they sway.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use respected figures, professionals, or institutions (physicians, experts, associations) to endorse or appear to endorse a position so the public will follow; example: surveying physicians and publicizing their recommendation to promote bacon and eggs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate tie-ins and cross-media strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 'tie-up' or 'tie-in' strategy: link one venue or occasion for promoting a product to another, and possibly to a third or fourth, including holidays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine radio, newspaper, department-store exhibitions, and timing (e.g., Thrift Week) to amplify a campaign; plan interconnected promotional venues to reinforce the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply behavioral and social science (engineering of consent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use psychology and other social sciences to design public persuasion campaigns; Bernays called this the 'engineering of consent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand group psychology, crowd behavior, psychoanalytic insights (Freud, Pavlov) and apply them scientifically to shape opinions, tastes and habits; treat PR work as a practicing social scientist using sociology, social psychology, anthropology, history, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accuracy, candor, and educational merit when using schools or public institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The school may disseminate information concerning scientific facts; such propaganda activities, if they are accurate and candid, are in no way reprehensible, provided the school authorities accept or reject such offers carefully on their educational merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When supplying educational materials (pictures, charts, demonstrations) to schools or institutions, ensure content is accurate, candid, and pedagogically justified; institutions must vet offers for true educational value to avoid covert commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target fundamental human appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: No matter how sophisticated, how cynical the public may become about publicity methods, it must respond to the basic appeals, because it will always need food, crave amusement, long for beauty, respond to leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft messages that connect to universal human needs and desires (food, entertainment, aesthetics, leadership) as reliable levers of persuasion across audience sophistication levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt to changing public sophistication and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If the public becomes more intelligent in its commercial demands, commercial firms will meet the new standards. If it becomes weary of the old methods used to persuade it... appeals will be presented more intelligently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor audience awareness and evolve techniques and standards accordingly; higher public scrutiny demands more sophisticated, often more ethical, approaches to persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain duty to society above client demands
rubrics_metrics.description: A public relations counsel 'must never accept a retainer or assume a position which puts his duty to the groups he represents above his duty to society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize ethical limits: do not prioritize client interests when they conflict with broader societal welfare; be aware propaganda can subvert democracy and thus has serious political consequences (e.g., Nazi misuse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize risks of propaganda and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays acknowledged potential danger in mass technique for distributing ideas: propaganda can be used to subvert democracy as easily as to resolve conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the political and social risks of manipulative campaigns; historical examples (use by Goebbels/Nazis, Operation PBSUCCESS in Guatemala) show that techniques of persuasion can have destructive outcomes—exercise caution and ethical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surveys and manufactured consensus carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct surveys of authorities and publicize the results to suggest expert endorsement (example: bacon-and-eggs breakfast promoted by surveying physicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys and targeted dissemination to influencers can manufacture perceived consensus; practitioners should note both the effectiveness and the ethical implications of presenting engineered endorsements as unbiased expert opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer news-media framing and earned media tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Bernays convinced industries that the news, not advertising, was the best medium to carry their message to an unsuspecting public and secured coverage free of charge by contriving events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that editors and reporters will cover (stunts, third-party endorsements, timed events) to obtain earned media; be mindful this blurs lines between news and publicity and raises ethical transparency issues.
